name: Adversarial Machine Learning
description: Adversarial examples, poisoning, backdoors, evasion, and robustness of ML models.

ccs.narrative:
Adversarial machine learning grew from a niche CCS topic in 2018 into one of the conference's dominant threads. The opening papers established both attack primitives and measurement frameworks: Deep Fingerprinting: Undermining Website Fingerprinting Defenses with Deep Learning (CCS 2018) used CNNs to break Tor defenses, while Property Inference Attacks on Fully Connected Neural Networks using Permutation Invariant Representations (CCS 2018) showed that models leak global dataset properties. LEMNA: Explaining Deep Learning based Security Applications (CCS 2018) simultaneously raised the question of whether these complex models could be trusted at all.

In 2019, the battlefield expanded to physical systems and backdoors. Adversarial Sensor Attack on LiDAR-based Perception in Autonomous Driving (CCS 2019) spoofed LIDAR to inject phantom obstacles into self-driving pipelines, a landmark that made physical adversarial attacks a first-class concern. ABS: Scanning Neural Networks for Back-doors by Artificial Brain Stimulation (CCS 2019) and Latent Backdoor Attacks on Deep Neural Networks (CCS 2019) framed the backdoor arms race that would define 2020-2023.

By 2023-2024, generative AI became the new terrain. Narcissus: A Practical Clean-Label Backdoor Attack with Limited Information (CCS 2023) showed backdoors survive even clean-label constraints, DE-FAKE: Detection and Attribution of Fake Images Generated by Text-to-Image Generation Models (CCS 2023) turned attribution into a forensics problem, and Do Users Write More Insecure Code with AI Assistants? (CCS 2023) quantified the real-world security cost of AI code generation.

milestones.title: Deep Fingerprinting: Undermining Website Fingerprinting Defenses with Deep Learning
milestones.note: Demonstrated deep learning breaks state-of-the-art Tor traffic defenses, raising the bar for anonymity tools.

milestones.title: Property Inference Attacks on Fully Connected Neural Networks using Permutation Invariant Representations
milestones.note: Established property inference as a distinct privacy threat extracting global dataset statistics from models.

milestones.title: Machine Learning with Membership Privacy using Adversarial Regularization
milestones.note: Pioneered adversarial regularization as a training-time defense against membership inference attacks.

milestones.title: Adversarial Sensor Attack on LiDAR-based Perception in Autonomous Driving
milestones.note: First practical LiDAR spoofing attack against autonomous vehicle perception, bridging adversarial ML and physical security.

milestones.title: ABS: Scanning Neural Networks for Back-doors by Artificial Brain Stimulation
milestones.note: Introduced neuron stimulation as a scalable method to detect trojaned neural networks.

milestones.title: Latent Backdoor Attacks on Deep Neural Networks
milestones.note: Showed backdoors survive transfer learning from teacher to student models, vastly expanding the threat surface.

milestones.title: Backdoor Pre-trained Models Can Transfer to All
milestones.note: Proved backdoors in pre-trained NLP encoders persist across any downstream fine-tuning task.

milestones.title: Narcissus: A Practical Clean-Label Backdoor Attack with Limited Information
milestones.note: Achieved practical clean-label backdoors that evade human inspection with minimal adversarial knowledge.

ndss.narrative:
ML security at NDSS has tracked the field's maturation from basic adversarial examples to complex attacks and defenses spanning the full ML pipeline. Trojaning Attack on Neural Networks (NDSS 2018) established the backdoor threat model that has since spawned hundreds of follow-on papers. NIC (NDSS 2019) responded with the first neural-network invariant checking framework for detecting adversarial samples at inference time, demonstrating that defenses could keep pace with attacks.

The 2020–2022 cohort tackled federated learning and network-level applications simultaneously. Manipulating the Byzantine (NDSS 2021) and DeepSight (NDSS 2022) defined the attack-defense frontier in distributed learning; meanwhile papers applying ML to security tasks—traffic classification, binary analysis, anomaly detection—appeared in parallel, blurring the line between ML-as-target and ML-as-tool.

By 2023–2025 the agenda bifurcated. One track continued hardening ML models against adversarial inputs and poisoning (Do We Really Need to Design New Byzantine-robust Aggregation Rules?, NDSS 2025). The other explored ML as a potent offensive and analytic instrument: Detecting Unknown Encrypted Malicious Traffic (NDSS 2023) and Invisible Reflections (NDSS 2024) used learned models to identify threats and mount physical attacks. The throughline across seven years is an arms race in which attacks and defenses co-evolve, with neither side achieving a durable advantage.

milestones.title: Trojaning Attack on Neural Networks
milestones.note: Trojans neural networks by crafting triggers and retraining, causing targeted misbehavior on inputs with the trigger.

milestones.title: NIC: Detecting Adversarial Samples with Neural Network Invariant Checking
milestones.note: Detects adversarial examples by checking neural network invariants across layers to flag inputs that cause DNN misclassification.

milestones.title: DeepBinDiff: Learning Program-Wide Code Representations for Binary Diffing
milestones.note: Presents DeepBinDiff, learning program-wide code representations for fine-grained basic-block-level binary diffing.

milestones.title: Manipulating the Byzantine: Optimizing Model Poisoning Attacks and Defenses for Federated Learning
milestones.note: Optimizes model-poisoning attacks against federated learning and evaluates corresponding byzantine-robust defenses.

milestones.title: DeepSight: Mitigating Backdoor Attacks in Federated Learning Through Deep Model Inspection
milestones.note: Mitigates backdoor poisoning in federated learning through deep inspection of submitted model updates.

milestones.title: Detecting Unknown Encrypted Malicious Traffic in Real Time via Flow Interaction Graph Analysis
milestones.note: HyperVision detects unknown encrypted malicious traffic in real time using unsupervised learning over flow interaction graphs.

milestones.title: Invisible Reflections: Leveraging Infrared Laser Reflections to Target Traffic Sign Perception
milestones.note: Uses invisible infrared laser reflections to manipulate autonomous vehicle traffic sign perception.

milestones.title: Do We Really Need to Design New Byzantine-robust Aggregation Rules?
milestones.note: Questions whether new Byzantine-robust aggregation rules are needed to defend federated learning against poisoning attacks.

sp.narrative:
Adversarial ML at IEEE S&P opened in 2018 with formal certification and empirical attack construction. AI2: Safety and Robustness Certification of Neural Networks with Abstract Interpretation (S&P 2018) applied program-analysis techniques to prove network robustness properties, while Manipulating Machine Learning: Poisoning Attacks and Countermeasures for Regression Learning (S&P 2018) provided rigorous threat modeling for training-time attacks. Stealing Hyperparameters in Machine Learning (S&P 2018) extended model-theft attacks beyond weights to the hyperparameter space.

2019 marked a turn toward backdoors and robustness. Neural Cleanse: Identifying and Mitigating Backdoor Attacks in Neural Networks (S&P 2019) established trigger reverse-engineering as the canonical defense template. Certified Robustness to Adversarial Examples with Differential Privacy (S&P 2019) connected DP-based smoothing to provable robustness certificates, spawning a large follow-on literature. DEEPSEC: A Uniform Platform for Security Analysis of Deep Learning Model (S&P 2019) offered the first systematic evaluation framework for comparing attacks and defenses.

The 2020-2021 wave made attacks more realistic and physical. HopSkipJumpAttack: A Query-Efficient Decision-Based Attack (S&P 2020) removed the gradient-access assumption, and Intriguing Properties of Adversarial ML Attacks in the Problem Space (S&P 2020) highlighted the gap between feature-space and real-world transferability. Invisible for both Camera and LiDAR: Security of Multi-Sensor Fusion based Perception in Autonomous Driving (S&P 2021) brought physical adversarial examples to safety-critical AV perception.

By 2022-2024, the community scrutinized its own threat models. Back to the Drawing Board: A Critical Evaluation of Poisoning Attacks on Production Federated Learning (S&P 2022) showed most proposed attacks fail under realistic server configurations. Poisoning Web-Scale Training Datasets is Practical (S&P 2024) demonstrated dataset poisoning at foundation-model scale via Wikipedia and web-crawl manipulation, shifting the conversation from hypothetical to operational.

uss.narrative:
The earliest papers in this list, all from USENIX Security 2018, show a field still mapping out the basic shape of the threat. Several works asked how machine learning could be attacked or formally trusted: "When Does Machine Learning FAIL? Generalized Transferability for Evasion and Poisoning Attacks" (USENIX 2018) unified evasion and poisoning under a single transferability framework, while "Formal Security Analysis of Neural Networks using Symbolic Intervals" (USENIX 2018) pushed in the opposite direction, trying to prove robustness guarantees rather than just demonstrate breakage. At the same time, attacks were already leaving the image domain and hitting real systems, from speech ("CommanderSong: A Systematic Approach for Practical Adversarial Voice Recognition", USENIX 2018) to transfer-learning pipelines ("With Great Training Comes Great Vulnerability: Practical Attacks against Transfer Learning", USENIX 2018). A notable inversion of the threat model also appeared early: "Turning Your Weakness Into a Strength: Watermarking Deep Neural Networks by Backdooring" (USENIX 2018) repurposed backdoors as a defensive ownership tool.

The 2019-2020 period marks a shift from digital perturbations to the physical and hardware substrate of ML systems. "Terminal Brain Damage" (USENIX 2019) and "DeepHammer" (USENIX 2020) showed that flipping a handful of bits in memory via Rowhammer could destroy a network's accuracy, attacking the model where it actually runs rather than at its input. In parallel, attacks moved into the physical sensing pipeline: "Seeing is Not Believing: Camouflage Attacks on Image Scaling Algorithms" (USENIX 2019) exploited preprocessing, and "Towards Robust LiDAR-based Perception in Autonomous Driving" (USENIX 2020) demonstrated black-box sensor spoofing against self-driving perception. This era also reframed adversarial techniques as protective tools for ordinary users, most prominently "Fawkes: Protecting Privacy against Unauthorized Deep Learning Models" (USENIX 2020), which cloaked photos to defeat facial recognition scrapers.

By 2021-2022 the community converged on backdoor and poisoning attacks as a central, deployment-relevant concern, especially in pipelines that ingest untrusted data. "Explanation-Guided Backdoor Poisoning Attacks Against Malware Classifiers" (USENIX 2021) used model explanations to craft stealthy poison in crowdsourced threat feeds, and the threat broadened beyond images into text ("T-Miner", USENIX 2021; "Hidden Trigger Backdoor Attack on NLP Models via Linguistic Style Manipulation", USENIX 2022) and into distributed training ("FLAME: Taming Backdoors in Federated Learning", USENIX 2022). Defenses matured alongside, with work like "CADE: Detecting and Explaining Concept Drift Samples for Security Applications" (USENIX 2021) tackling the drift that makes security classifiers brittle over time.

Most recently, attention has tracked the rise of generative models and large language models. "Extracting Training Data from Diffusion Models" (USENIX 2023) showed that image generators memorize and leak their training data, while "Glaze: Protecting Artists from Style Mimicry by Text-to-Image Models" (USENIX 2023) again turned adversarial perturbations into a protective shield, this time for artists rather than faces, echoing Fawkes years earlier. The frontier has now reached LLM safety directly, with "Making Them Ask and Answer: Jailbreaking Large Language Models in Few Queries via Disguise and Reconstruction" (USENIX 2024) demonstrating efficient query-based jailbreaks. Across six years the area has moved from proving and breaking image classifiers toward securing the full lifecycle of generative and foundation models.

top4.narrative:
The earliest papers in this list, from 2018, established the core threat surface of adversarial machine learning across security venues. Two themes dominated. First, the discovery that shared, pre-trained models could be weaponized: "Trojaning Attack on Neural Networks" (NDSS 2018) showed an attacker could implant hidden triggers into a network, while "Manipulating Machine Learning: Poisoning Attacks and Countermeasures for Regression Learning" (S&P 2018) formalized training-time poisoning. Second, a defensive countercurrent emerged that tried to put guarantees under these brittle models, with "AI2: Safety and Robustness Certification of Neural Networks with Abstract Interpretation" (S&P 2018) and "Formal Security Analysis of Neural Networks using Symbolic Intervals" (USENIX 2018) bringing program-analysis tools to certify robustness. The same year also broadened the attack catalog beyond images, into voice ("CommanderSong", USENIX 2018), website fingerprinting ("Deep Fingerprinting", CCS 2018), and model/privacy theft ("Stealing Hyperparameters in Machine Learning", S&P 2018).

A clear shift toward backdoors and detection happened in 2019. "Neural Cleanse: Identifying and Mitigating Backdoor Attacks in Neural Networks" (S&P 2019) became the reference point for reverse-engineering hidden triggers, complemented by "ABS: Scanning Neural Networks for Back-doors by Artificial Brain Stimulation" (CCS 2019) and stealthier variants like "Latent Backdoor Attacks on Deep Neural Networks" (CCS 2019). At the same time, certified defenses matured beyond abstract interpretation into randomized smoothing via "Certified Robustness to Adversarial Examples with Differential Privacy" (S&P 2019). A second important move was attacks leaving the digital domain: "Adversarial Sensor Attack on LiDAR-based Perception in Autonomous Driving" (CCS 2019) opened a long line of physical-world autonomous-vehicle work, continued in "Towards Robust LiDAR-based Perception" (USENIX 2020) and "Invisible for both Camera and LiDAR" (S&P 2021). Researchers also noticed the attack-defense arms race feeding back on itself, with "Privacy Risks of Securing Machine Learning Models against Adversarial Examples" (CCS 2019) showing robustness can worsen privacy leakage.

From 2020 the field grew more rigorous and more practical. "HopSkipJumpAttack" (S&P 2020) made decision-based black-box attacks query-efficient, and "Intriguing Properties of Adversarial ML Attacks in the Problem Space" (S&P 2020) pushed the community to reason about realizable objects rather than abstract perturbations. Federated learning became a major battleground, with "Manipulating the Byzantine: Optimizing Model Poisoning Attacks and Defenses for Federated Learning" (NDSS 2021) and "FLAME: Taming Backdoors in Federated Learning" (USENIX 2022), followed by a sobering reality check in "Back to the Drawing Board: A Critical Evaluation of Poisoning Attacks on Production Federated Learning" (S&P 2022), which questioned whether these attacks matter in deployment.

Most recently, the center of gravity moved to large generative models and web-scale training. "Extracting Training Data from Diffusion Models" (USENIX 2023) showed that generative models memorize and leak their training images, while "Glaze: Protecting Artists from Style Mimicry" (USENIX 2023) turned adversarial perturbations into a protective tool for human creators, echoing the earlier privacy-shield idea of "Fawkes" (USENIX 2020). "Poisoning Web-Scale Training Datasets is Practical" (S&P 2024) closed the loop by demonstrating that the foundational assumption of clean internet-scraped data is itself vulnerable. Across these venues the area has evolved from proof-of-concept attacks on single classifiers to a mature discipline spanning certified defenses, physical-world and federated settings, and the privacy and integrity of today's largest generative systems.
